guide.title: Sunset Park, Brooklyn: The Hill, the Terminal, Eighth Avenue
guide.intro: Sunset Park is named for the hilltop the City of Brooklyn acquired on May 15, 1891: four blocks between Fifth and Seventh Avenues, extended to 44th Street in 1904, on a roughly 164-foot rise in the Harbor Hill Moraine. The first European settlement here came in 1636, when Willem Adriaenszen Bennett and Jacques Bentyn bought 936 acres, and the area was still primarily agricultural in the 1830s. Development followed the transit lines: the Fifth Avenue elevated opened in 1889 and reached a 65th Street terminal on October 1, 1893, and the Fourth Avenue subway opened to 59th Street on June 21, 1915. The waterfront filled with Irving T. Bush's terminal complex and, from 1918, Cass Gilbert's Brooklyn Army Terminal. In the 1980s Sunset Park became the location of the borough's first Chinatown, along Eighth Avenue.

sections.heading: Farmland, then a working waterfront
sections.body:
Irving T. Bush assembled Bush Terminal along the shore in two named portions, one running roughly from 32nd to 41st Streets and the other from 40th to 51st Streets. At its peak the complex employed about 35,000 people by 1928.

The Brooklyn Army Terminal followed, at 58th Street. Cass Gilbert designed the supply base; construction began on May 15, 1918 and finished in September 1919, and it is described as the largest military supply base in the United States through World War II. A decommissioning ceremony was held on December 9, 1966 and Army operations ceased on January 1, 1967. The city finalised its purchase in July 1981 for $8.5 million and started the renovation in 1985.

Inland, the neighborhood kept its late-nineteenth and early-twentieth-century fabric. Alku and Alku Toinen, built in 1916 at 816 and 826 43rd Street for the neighborhood's Finnish community, are recognised as the first purpose-built non-profit housing cooperatives in New York State and were listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 20, 2019. A block of 40th Street, at the Imatra Society building at 740 40th Street, was co-named Finlandia Street in 1991. St. Michael's parish was founded in 1870 and its present church at 352 42nd Street was completed in 1905 to designs by Raymond F. Almirall; it is sometimes called Brooklyn's own Sacre-Coeur. The Basilica of Our Lady of Perpetual Help, at 526 59th Street, was begun in 1907 and completed in 1928 to designs by Franz Joseph Untersee, and was elevated to minor basilica by the pontifical decree Quamquam Christianus on September 15, 1969.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Sunset Park sits on the BMT Fourth Avenue Line, and four of its stations are in the neighborhood. The 36th Street station is served by the R, D and N at all times. The 45th Street, 53rd Street and 59th Street stations are served by the R at all times; N trains call at 59th Street at all times, and at 45th Street and 53rd Street on late nights and limited rush-hour trips.

NYC Ferry's South Brooklyn route calls at the Sunset Park/Brooklyn Army Terminal landing, Pier 4, 140 58th Street. Free public parking is available at Pier 4 for Brooklyn Army Terminal visitors and ferry riders.

sections.heading: Two commercial avenues
sections.body:
In the 1980s Sunset Park became the location of the borough's first Chinatown, which runs along Eighth Avenue and is the borough's largest, with grocery stores, restaurants, Buddhist temples and bakeries. The Choi Yung Grocery opened in 1983 at 5517 Fort Hamilton Parkway, and the Winley Supermarket opened in 1986 at 5523 8th Avenue; Winley is credited with drawing more Asian visitors to the strip after roughly 90 percent of Eighth Avenue storefronts had been abandoned by 1988. Canton House Restaurant, the first Cantonese seafood restaurant on Eighth Avenue, opened in 1985. The corridor was settled first by Cantonese immigrants and is increasingly home to Fujianese and Wenzhounese immigrants. How far north and south it reaches is not settled. Addresses are firmer: Great Taste Dumpling is at 4317 8th Avenue.

Fifth Avenue carries the other one, a corridor of Mexican, Guatemalan and Colombian restaurants and bakeries. Its ends are likewise unsettled; the establishments trading along it run at least between the 4000 and 5500 blocks, Tacos Matamoros among them at 4508 5th Avenue.

The change on both avenues followed a long decline on the waterfront that began in earnest with the Brooklyn Army Terminal's 1966 closure.

faq.question: How do I get to Sunset Park?
faq.answer: By subway, the 36th Street station is served by the R, D and N; 45th Street, 53rd Street and 59th Street are served by the R, with N service at 59th Street at all times and at 45th and 53rd Streets on late nights and limited rush-hour trips. NYC Ferry's South Brooklyn route calls at the Sunset Park/Brooklyn Army Terminal landing at Pier 4, 140 58th Street.

faq.question: Is Sunset Park a neighborhood or a park?
faq.answer: Both. The park sits between Fifth and Seventh Avenues from 41st to 44th Streets, covers about 24.5 acres, and gave the neighborhood around it its name after the City of Brooklyn acquired the original four blocks on May 15, 1891.

faq.question: Can visitors get inside the Brooklyn Army Terminal?
faq.answer: Public interior tours have been offered through Turnstile Tours since 2013, and NYC Ferry has served the terminal since May 2017. The complex is a working light-manufacturing and commercial site, so check the terminal's own site before going.

faq.question: How far does the Eighth Avenue Chinatown run?
faq.answer: Its northern and southern ends are not settled. What is firm is that it is the borough's first and largest Chinatown, with grocery stores, restaurants, Buddhist temples and bakeries along Eighth Avenue.

faq.question: Is the Sunset Park Courthouse open to the public?
faq.answer: No. The 1930-1931 building by Mortimer Dickerson Metcalfe was designated a New York City landmark on June 26, 2001, but it has served as an NYPD applicant-processing centre since a 1996 renovation, so only the exterior can be seen.

faq.question: Is there anywhere to stay in Sunset Park?
faq.answer: Yes. The Best Western Plus Prospect Park Hotel holds an active city hotel licence at 764 4th Avenue, inside the neighborhood. A second licensed hotel trades as Day's Inn at 437 39th Street.

places.name: Sunset Park
places.address: Between 5th and 7th Avenues, 41st-44th Streets, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: The 24.5-acre park that gave the neighborhood its name, on a roughly 164-foot hill in the Harbor Hill Moraine. The City of Brooklyn acquired the original four blocks on May 15, 1891 and the park was expanded to 44th Street in 1904.
places.history: The Sunset Play Center, the park's pool and bathhouse, was designated an individual New York City landmark on July 24, 2007.

places.name: Bush Terminal Piers Park
places.address: Between 43rd and 50th Streets on the waterfront, Brooklyn, NY
places.summary: A waterfront park built on the former Bush Terminal piers. Its 43rd Street entrance opened in November 2014 and its 50th Street entrance in July 2017.
places.history: The park covers about 24 acres between 43rd and 50th Streets, with a pedestrian and bike path, baseball and soccer fields, tidal ponds, a wooded area and pier access.

places.name: Industry City
places.summary: A 35-acre redevelopment of part of the former Bush Terminal complex, running roughly from 32nd to 41st Streets on the waterfront. It has petanque courts, event space and a climbing gym that opened in 2024.

places.name: Japan Village
places.summary: A Japanese food hall and marketplace inside Industry City, holding the Sunrise Mart grocery and several dining stalls. It runs an annual Summer Festival.

places.name: Brooklyn Army Terminal
places.summary: Cass Gilbert's United States Army supply base, built between May 1918 and September 1919 and described as the largest military supply base in the United States through World War II. It is now a city-owned light-manufacturing and commercial complex.
places.history: A decommissioning ceremony was held on December 9, 1966 and Army operations ceased on January 1, 1967. The city finalised its purchase in July 1981 for $8.5 million and began renovating the complex in 1985. Public interior tours have been offered through Turnstile Tours since 2013, and NYC Ferry has served the terminal since May 2017.

places.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Perpetual Help
places.summary: A church begun in 1907 and completed in 1928 to designs by Franz Joseph Untersee, elevated to minor basilica by the pontifical decree Quamquam Christianus on September 15, 1969.
places.history: The parish is now predominantly Hispanic and Chinese, with Masses celebrated in English, Spanish, Chinese and Vietnamese.

places.name: St. Michael's Church
places.summary: A Roman Catholic church whose parish was founded in 1870 and whose present building was completed in 1905 to designs by Raymond F. Almirall. It is sometimes called Brooklyn's own Sacre-Coeur.
places.history: The parish remains active; the parochial school attached to it closed in 2005.

places.name: Alku and Alku Toinen
places.summary: Two 1916 apartment buildings raised for the neighborhood's Finnish community and recognised as the first purpose-built non-profit housing cooperatives in New York State. They were listed on the National Register of Historic Places on May 20, 2019.
places.history: Both are occupied private cooperative apartment buildings, so only their exteriors can be seen.

places.name: Sunset Park Courthouse
places.summary: A courthouse built in 1930-1931 to designs by Mortimer Dickerson Metcalfe and designated a New York City landmark on June 26, 2001. Since a 1996 renovation it has housed the NYPD's applicant-processing centre, so it is not a visitor site; the exterior is what there is to see.
